world_behind.title: A burden against a city not yet dangerous
world_behind.text: Babylon was a secondary power when Isaiah spoke; Assyria was the empire. The oracle names a future oppressor, and Lehi's family fled Jerusalem in the generation Babylon finally took it. Nephi is copying a prophecy about the very city that destroyed the home he left.

world_behind.title: Sanctified ones for a war
world_behind.text: Verse 3 calls the invading army God's sanctified and mighty ones, language usually reserved for worshippers. Ancient warfare was consecrated business, with troops set apart before a campaign, so the vocabulary is not a compliment to the Medes so much as a claim about who commissioned them.

world_behind.title: The day of the Lord
world_behind.text: The phrase had a settled meaning by Isaiah's time: a day when God acts publicly and decisively. The block has used it before against Judah's high things. Here it is turned outward at an empire, and the pattern established earlier holds, since what comes down is again everything elevated.

world_behind.title: Sky signs
world_behind.text: Sun, moon, stars, and constellations all fail in verse 10, and the earth moves out of its place in verse 13. In the ancient world the sky was the one reliable thing, the calendar and compass both. Removing it is a way of saying that the framework people navigate by is itself under judgment.

world_behind.title: The Medes
world_behind.text: Verse 17 names the people who would eventually take Babylon, and the detail given about them is economic: they do not care about silver and gold. An invader who cannot be bought off is the worst kind for a wealthy city, and it is the only thing the chapter says about their character.

world_behind.title: Ruins full of animals
world_behind.text: The final picture is a site abandoned even by shepherds, occupied by desert creatures. Ancient curses against cities often ended this way, and the force of it is commercial as much as eerie: a place where no caravan camps and no flock is folded has stopped being a place at all.

words.text: A standard raised where troops can see it, the same object the block has called an ensign twice already. Here it is lifted on a high mountain to gather an army against Babylon. Three raisings now in this block, for an invasion, for a gathering, and for a siege, and the pole itself never changes.

An older form of arrogance, and it is paired with haughtiness in the same verse. The chapter's stated targets are the world's evil and the wicked's iniquity, and then these two: the arrogancy of the proud and the haughtiness of the terrible. Even against an empire, the specific charge is height.

An ingot, a cast bar of gold. Ophir was the far source of the finest gold known to Israel, so the wedge of Ophir is the most valuable object a hearer could picture. The verse's promise is that people will become scarcer than that, which is a statement about depopulation rather than about human worth.

Mournful, full of grief. It describes the creatures that occupy the ruined houses, and it is an odd word for animals, since the grief is in the sound they make rather than in what they feel. The verse names a house by what can be heard in it.

An older rendering for a large desert or marsh creature, jackal or serpent depending on the passage. The word closes the chapter's list of new tenants, and its placement is deliberate: dragons in the pleasant palaces, the least civilized thing in the most civilized room.

phrases.term: mine anger is not upon them that rejoice in my highness
phrases.text: The King James reads the clause the other way: God calls his mighty ones "for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness" (Isa. 13:3), which makes the rejoicers the instruments of the anger. This reading inserts a negation and exempts them from it. One word divides the sentence into two groups, those under the anger and those who rejoice in God's highness, and it is the first mercy in a chapter that otherwise has none until its last line.

phrases.term: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them
phrases.text: The King James adds a comparison the record does not carry: "they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth" (Isa. 13:8). Without it the verse runs straight from pangs to amazement to faces like flames, all of them descriptions of a body reacting. The dropped clause is the only figure in the passage, and its absence leaves the terror literal.

The verse is often read as a promise about human value, and the context makes it grimmer than that. After verse 11's punishing and before verse 13's shaking, making a man more precious than gold means there will be very few men left. Scarcity, not worth, is what raises the price.

phrases.term: Every one that is proud shall be thrust through
phrases.text: The King James has "Every one that is found" (Isa. 13:15), which makes the killing indiscriminate, and "every one that is joined unto them" for the second clause. This reading names both groups by character instead: the proud, and those joined to the wicked. What was a description of a massacre becomes a description of a judgment, and the difference is two substitutions.

phrases.term: as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah
phrases.text: The comparison is chosen for completeness rather than for the sin involved. Sodom's overthrow left nothing to rebuild and nobody to return, which is exactly what the next three verses describe. The record's readers had already heard the same city named in the block when Jerusalem's own countenance was said to declare its sin.

phrases.term: I will be merciful unto my people
phrases.text: The chapter's last line does not exist in the King James text, which ends with Babylon's days not being prolonged. Here a whole sentence follows: destruction speedily, mercy to God's people, and the wicked perishing. Twenty-two verses of unbroken judgment close on a promise, and the addition turns an oracle against one city into a statement about two outcomes.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: An army summoned by signal
verses.text: A banner on a mountain, a raised voice, a hand waved, and then the troops are identified as God's sanctified and mighty ones. The chapter opens by making an invasion a commissioned act, and it takes three verses to do what the Assyrian chapter took a whole argument to establish: the empire is the instrument.

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: The noise before the sight
verses.text: What arrives first is sound, a multitude in the mountains, a tumultuous noise of kingdoms. Only then are the weapons named, and they are "the weapons of his indignation" (v. 5). The army comes from the end of heaven, which is to say from beyond anywhere a hearer could point to.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: What the day does to a body
verses.text: Hands go faint, hearts melt, pangs take hold, faces turn to flame. Nothing in these verses describes destruction of property. The day of the Lord is registered in the body first, and the last detail is that people look at each other in amazement, which means nobody has an explanation.

verses.label: v. 9–13
verses.title: The sky goes out
verses.text: Stars, sun, moon, constellations, all withholding light, and then the earth itself moving. Between those two cosmic verses sits the reason, stated in ordinary moral terms: the world punished for evil, arrogancy stopped, haughtiness laid down. The frame of the universe is disturbed over human pride.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: A city taken
verses.text: The images turn domestic and brutal: people scattering like a chased animal, everyone running for his own country, and then children, houses, and wives. Isaiah does not soften any of it, and the record does not either. What the chapter promises about Babylon it describes without flinching.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: An enemy who cannot be bought
verses.text: The Medes are named, and the one fact given is that silver and gold will not interest them. For a city whose defense had always been its wealth, this is the sentence that makes the rest inevitable, and it is followed by the comparison to Sodom.

verses.label: v. 20–22
verses.title: New tenants, and a last line
verses.text: Never inhabited, no Arabian pitching a tent, no shepherd folding a flock, and then animals in the palaces. The chapter appears to end there, as the King James does. This reading adds one more sentence, and it is about mercy to God's people, which changes what the whole oracle was for.

chapter.title: The block turns outward
chapter.text: Chapters 12 through 22 aimed at Judah, Jerusalem, and the house of David. This one aims at Babylon, and the criteria do not change: arrogancy, haughtiness, pride. Isaiah applies the same standard to an empire that he applied to his own capital, which is what makes the standard credible.

chapter.title: Two variants pull the same direction
chapter.text: The negation at verse 3 exempts those who rejoice in God's highness, and the substitution at verse 15 makes the slain the proud rather than the found. Both changes convert indiscriminate destruction into judgment with criteria. Neither softens the outcome; both give it a reason.

chapter.title: The added sentence reframes the chapter
chapter.text: Ending on mercy to God's people rather than on Babylon's short days makes the oracle part of a larger promise instead of a self-contained curse. Every other chapter in this block ends where its Bible counterpart ends. This one does not, and the difference is the last thing a reader takes away.

chapter.title: Cosmic and domestic, alternating
chapter.text: Sun and stars in verse 10, children and houses in verse 16; the earth removed from its place in verse 13, an Arabian's tent in verse 20. Isaiah keeps descending from the sky to the street, which is how the chapter avoids becoming abstract despite its scale.

chapter.title: Nephi's own city fell to this one
chapter.text: Babylon took Jerusalem within a few years of his family's departure, and Lehi had preached that it would. Copying an oracle promising Babylon's own fall puts his people's story inside a longer sequence: the city that ended their old world is itself under sentence.

chapter.title: A day named and never dated
chapter.text: The chapter says the day of the Lord is at hand, that her time is near, that her day will not be prolonged, and gives no year. That combination has governed the whole block, and it is what allows the same chapter to be read about the Medes and about a day still coming.

applications.title: Take the second phrase seriously
applications.text: Rejoicing in God's highness is offered here as a description of a real group of people. Ask when you last took actual pleasure in God being greater than you, rather than merely conceding it.

applications.title: Watch what your body reports
applications.text: This chapter registers the day of the Lord in hands, hearts, and faces before anything else. Notice where fear currently lives in your body, and treat that as information about what you actually believe is at stake.

applications.title: Test what cannot be bought
applications.text: Babylon's defense was wealth, and the Medes did not want it. Identify the protection you have been counting on, and ask what kind of trouble it would be useless against. Then decide whether you are prepared for that kind.

applications.title: Count the pride, not the sins
applications.text: The chapter's stated targets against a whole empire are arrogancy and haughtiness. Do the same audit on yourself: not a list of failures, but an honest look at where you consider yourself above correction.

applications.title: Do not skip the last sentence
applications.text: This oracle ends in mercy because a line was added that the Bible's version lacks. When a hard passage of scripture or a hard season seems to end in judgment, read to the actual end before concluding.

applications.title: Locate your Babylon
applications.text: Name the thing in your life that looks permanent, glorious, and unaccountable. Then read verses 20 through 22 with it in mind. The chapter's claim is not that such things are evil but that they are temporary.

questions.text: Do I rejoice in God's highness, or do I mostly want him to be useful to me?
What would it take for the day of the Lord to feel at hand rather than theoretical?
Where am I proud in a way I would defend if challenged?
If people became scarce, would I be missed for what I gave or only for what I held?
What am I trying to pay my way out of that will not accept payment?
Do I read God's warnings all the way to the mercy, or do I stop at the part that frightens me?
